pbt_gf30.notes: The connector-housing workhorse: stiff, dimensionally stable, solder-survivable and cheap for what it does. Values are dry and parallel to flow — transverse CTE is 2-3x — and glass-filled PBT warps if the fibre orientation is not thought about at the gate.

pet_gf30.notes: Stiffer, stronger and glossier than PBT-GF30 with better creep resistance hot, but PET crystallises slowly: it needs a mould above ~120 C or the part comes out amorphous, brittle and dimensionally unstable. Choose PBT-GF30 when the tool cannot run that hot.

ppo.notes: Never sold neat — PPE is blended with polystyrene (Noryl-type) to make it processable, and the blend ratio sets everything, so grades span roughly 100-140 C heat deflection. Near-zero water absorption and a very stable, low dielectric constant make it the choice for pump housings, water manifolds and electrical parts that must not move with humidity.

pc_gf20.notes: Glass more than doubles PC's stiffness and drops the CTE to roughly aluminium's — useful when a plastic housing must hold tolerance against a metal frame. It costs the transparency and, more importantly, the ductile high-energy impact behaviour that unfilled PC is usually specified for.

pc_abs.notes: Most of polycarbonate's heat resistance and notched impact with ABS's melt flow, cost and thick-section mouldability, and far less notch sensitivity than neat PC. The PC fraction (typically 50-70 %) sets where a grade lands, so read the specific datasheet. The standard automotive-interior and IT-housing material, and a common FDM engineering filament.

pctg.notes: Tougher and clearer than PETG in thick sections, with better resistance to detergents, disinfectants and lipids — the medical-device and drinkware copolyester. Amorphous, so it moulds without crystallisation control; CTE and thermal conductivity are omitted rather than guessed.
